h: Willows everywhere, once you start looking
p: Here's a little detail that unlocks the whole building. The name Sauchiehall comes from old Scots words meaning something like a meadow or alley of willows. Mackintosh ran with that idea, and the willow shape turns up all over the place, in the stylised trees, the patterns on the glass and the curves of the furniture. Once you've spotted it once, you'll see it everywhere, and it's a fun game for older kids too.

The building hasn't always been this loved. After Kate Cranston's day it went through all sorts of uses, including time as part of a department store. A charity bought it in 2014, and after a painstaking restoration it reopened in 2018, the year marking 150 years since Mackintosh's birth. Lots of the fittings had to be carefully recreated using old photographs and records, which tells you how much work went into what you're sitting in.

Glasgow is a dream for anyone who catches the Mackintosh bug. The Lighthouse, down a lane off Buchanan Street, was his first public building and has a tower you can climb for views over the rooftops. The Hunterian at the University of Glasgow has The Mackintosh House, a reassembly of his home's interiors. And across in Bellahouston Park, House for an Art Lover was built later from designs he drew up for a competition.
Plan an hour or so here if you're having tea and looking round the exhibition, a little longer if you're a proper design fan who wants to take it all in.
